title: Physics and architecture are easy, art and presentation is hard
author: Interesting-Bee-113
selftext:
I have three projects I am working on right now. The project depicted in the attached video is a game I am developing called I call Rover.

I feel like the game simulates physics very faithfully for the time being. There is an implementation I am working through right now that introduces tera-mechanics to the ground terrain. It's not something I can copy from another game because it's a system that my coding agents and I will have to invent. Basically, I want to model the ground as grains with inter-grain friction and pressure and resistance etc. Modeling the desired behavior in the simulation isn't the hard part. I am not worried about this implementation at all.  
  
The hard part is making it look good and convincing while it's happening. Hero assets, animation, texture, these are the hard parts. Those parts, I have burnt millions of tokens just to come up with assets and works that I am all too happy to scrap.

I have a working rally car physically modeled in the game and it's drivable, but the actual rendered asset I have for it offends my eyes almost. It's so primitive and crude. I tried getting set up on blender with the agent, but that honestly didn't produce much better results. 

And this is just one car, let alone the driver avatar and the animations for that.

I feel like, even with how advanced and sophisticated the models and agents are now, the art labor is still better in competent human hands at this point.

replies.author: Interesting-Bee-113
replies.body:
I don't

replies.author: the_vast_awaits
replies.body: I see, what development environment do you use then?

replies.author: Interesting-Bee-113
replies.body: It's a local-first, browser-native, no-build development environment: vanilla JavaScript and Three.js, served through localhost, with Git, deterministic Node/browser testing, AI-assisted implementation, and hands-on owner testing for final feel.

comments.author: Dull_Mention_7456
comments.body: I really like how real the suspension behaves. I prototyped a monster truck game but couldn't get to what you have here and then I gave up. Good job!

replies.author: Interesting-Bee-113
replies.body:
It was very difficult, but the trick was to model the suspension as real geometry. Then I had to add real components like ARB and anti-squat/anti-dive linkage to get the realistic behavior.

It started out with everything as authored scripts. Braking drops nose, throttle drops rear, right turns load left side suspension. 

Then then I refactored to having the engine model an actual dynamic vehicle load, which then made it critical to model almost everything a real truck has to be drivable and controlable.

Next post I'll upload with sound so you can hear the engine. The truck sounds a lot like a monster truck xD

And it is basically a mini monster truck. 1660 horsepower, 3 tons and an extremely exaggerated suspension travel distance.

I'd say circle back around to your projects some time. This game started out as a 2D side scroller I gave up on months ago.

replies.author: Interesting-Bee-113
replies.body:
Thank you.

I mean it is, technically complicated sure, but the simple thing is that the truck drives the way expectations says it should, for the most part.

I have driven a lot of off road, so I have a good corpus for how it ought to look and/or feel.

The physics implementations were mostly; why does the truck do this, what would a real truck do, and what do we want our truck to actually do, over and over again.

Also having a way to record telemetry, and show an agent who can underatand it helps 1000%
